title: test-0012-SCI-BIO-MOVEMENT
passage: Many people mistakenly believe that the human backbone is a single, stiff, long bone, but it is actually made of many small vertebrae stacked together. This structure allows us to bend and twist our bodies easily. Similarly, some think that bones are dead, rock-like structures, but they are living tissues that grow and repair themselves throughout our lives. At the places where our bones meet, we have joints. While we often think all joints allow movement, some, like those in our skull, are fixed and do not move at all. Between these bones, we find a smooth, flexible tissue called cartilage. It is not just found in the ears or nose; it acts as a cushion at joints to prevent bones from rubbing against each other. Furthermore, movement is not just about bones; it requires muscles. Muscles are found all over the body, not just in the arms or legs, and they work in pairs. One muscle pulls to move a bone, but it cannot push the bone back; a second muscle must pull in the opposite direction to return the bone to its original position. Understanding these systems helps us see how our body functions as a complex, living machine.
summary: Movement is not just about bones—it also needs muscles. One muscle pulls to move a bone, but it can't push it back. A second muscle must pull in the opposite direction to get the bone back to its original place.
